author: @studywithmara
title: 5 study habits backed by research
body:
1. Spaced repetition: review your notes after 1 day, 3 days, then a week. Your brain keeps what it revisits.

2. Active recall: close the book and quiz yourself. Struggling to remember is what makes it stick.

3. Interleaving: mix topics in one session instead of doing 3 hours of one subject.

4. Short breaks: 25 minutes of focus, 5 minutes off. Phone stays in another room.

5. Teach it: explain the lesson out loud like you are teaching a friend. Gaps show up fast.
why: Five research-backed techniques you can use at your next study session.

author: @factcheck.ph
title: How to check if a news photo is real
body:
Before you share a dramatic photo, take 30 seconds:

• Do a reverse image search. Old photos often get recycled as "breaking news."

• Look at the details: signs, weather, clothing. Do they match the place and date being claimed?

• Check who posted it first. A real news outlet or an anonymous page?

• Look for weird edges, warped hands or melted text. These are common signs of edited or AI-made images.

If you can't verify it, don't share it.
why: Teaches a 30-second check that stops you from spreading fake photos.

author: @weatherwatch.ph
title: PAGASA typhoon update: what to prepare
body:
A tropical depression may strengthen into a typhoon within 48 hours. Follow official PAGASA bulletins, not forwarded messages.

Go-bag checklist:
• Water (3 liters per person per day)
• Canned food and a manual can opener
• Flashlight, power bank, extra batteries
• Copies of IDs in a waterproof pouch
• Basic meds and a first-aid kit

Know your barangay's evacuation center and agree on a meeting point with your family.
why: Points you to official bulletins and gives a checklist that keeps your family safe.

author: @codewithjun
title: Free Python course for beginners
body:
Zero experience needed. The course has 6 weeks of short lessons, 20 minutes a day:

Week 1: Variables and printing
Week 2: If-statements and loops
Week 3: Lists and dictionaries
Week 4: Functions
Week 5: Reading files
Week 6: Build a mini budget tracker

Everything runs in your browser, so you don't need a laptop with special software. A school computer or phone works. Certificate included.
why: A free, step-by-step path to a real skill, with no catch.

author: @peso.smart
title: Budgeting tips for students on allowance
body:
Try the 50/30/20 split on your weekly allowance:

• 50% needs: fare, food, school supplies
• 30% wants: milk tea, games, hangouts
• 20% savings: put it aside the day you receive it

Other tips:
• Bring baon twice a week. It adds up fast.
• Track every spend for one week. You'll be surprised.
• Wait 24 hours before buying anything over ₱300.
why: Concrete money tips that actually fit a student allowance.

author: @sleepscience.daily
title: Why sleep matters before exams
body:
Pulling an all-nighter feels productive, but your brain stores memories while you sleep.

Students who sleep 7–9 hours before a test usually recall more than those who stay up cramming.

What helps:
• Stop screens 30 minutes before bed. The scroll keeps your brain wired.
• Review your hardest topic right before sleeping.
• Keep the same wake-up time, even on weekends.

Sleep is part of studying, not a break from it.
why: Explains how sleep helps memory, with easy steps you can try tonight.

author: @jobready.ph
title: First part-time job? Know your rights
body:
Landing your first job is exciting. Protect yourself:

• Never pay a "training fee" or "uniform deposit" to get hired. That's a common scam.
• Ask for your pay rate in writing, and keep every payslip.
• If you're 15–17, the law limits you to 8 hours a day, 40 hours a week, and no night shifts (10 PM–6 AM).
• Your school and studies come first. A good employer will work around your class schedule.

Not sure if an offer is legit? Ask your guidance office or a trusted adult before saying yes.
why: Practical rules that protect working students from scams and unfair hours.

author: @scholar.alerts
title: Is that scholarship offer legit? 4 checks
body:
Scholarship season brings real chances and fake ones. Before you send anything:

1. Legit scholarships never ask you to pay to apply.
2. Find the offer on the agency's or school's official website, not just a shared post.
3. Check the email address. Official offices don't use random free accounts.
4. Never send your full ID photos or bank details to a page you can't verify.

Save the official deadline in your calendar the moment you find it.
why: Helps you chase real scholarships while avoiding fake ones that steal your info.

author: @campus.wellbeing
title: Feeling burned out? Small steps that help
body:
Burnout isn't laziness. It's what happens when the load stays heavy for too long.

Small steps that help:
• Break tasks into 15-minute pieces and start with the easiest one.
• Move your body for 10 minutes. A walk counts.
• Protect your sleep, even during exam week.
• Talk to someone: a friend, family, or your school's guidance counselor.

If you feel overwhelmed or unsafe, the NCMH crisis hotline 1553 is free and open 24/7.
why: Kind, realistic advice plus a real hotline for when things get heavy.

author: @floodready.ph
title: What to do when your street floods
body:
Heavy rain again? Stay safe:

• Avoid wading through floodwater. It can hide open manholes and carry leptospirosis.
• If you had to wade and later get a fever or muscle pain, see a doctor right away and mention the flood.
• Switch off the main power before water reaches outlets.
• Move important papers and gadgets up high early.
• Follow your barangay's advisories on when to evacuate.
why: Clear safety steps for floods, including a health risk many people miss.

author: @newsliteracy.ph
title: Read past the headline: 3 quick questions
body:
Headlines are written to get clicks. Before you react or share, ask:

1. Who is the source? A named outlet or expert, or "sources say"?
2. When was it published? Old stories often come back as new.
3. What's missing? Numbers, names, the other side of the story?

If the article doesn't answer these, look for the same story from a second outlet.
why: Three questions that make you harder to fool with any headline.

author: @commute.tipid
title: Students get 20% off fare: don't forget your ID
body:
Students get a 20% discount on public transport fares like jeeps, buses and trains.

To claim it:
• Show your valid school ID when you pay.
• Ask politely if the driver or conductor forgets.
• The discount applies on school days and weekends.

That's real savings on a daily commute. Add it to your budget plan.
why: A small, real money-saver most students can use every day.

author: @resume.basics
title: Your first resume in 15 minutes
body:
No work experience? You still have plenty to put down.

• Contact info: a simple, professional email address.
• Education: school, strand or course, year level.
• Skills: computer skills, languages, anything you're good at.
• Activities: org roles, school projects, volunteering.
• Keep it to one page, and save it as a PDF.

Ask a teacher to look it over before you send it.
why: A simple template you can use this week for OJT or a part-time job.

author: @digisafe.ph
title: Turn on 2-step verification today
body:
Passwords leak. 2-step verification means a stolen password alone isn't enough to get into your account.

• Go to your account's security settings and turn on 2-step verification.
• Use an authenticator app if you can. It's safer than text codes.
• Save your backup codes somewhere offline.
• Never share a login code with anyone, even someone claiming to be "support."

Start with your email. It's the key to resetting everything else.
why: One five-minute setting that protects all your accounts.

author: @groupwork.tips
title: How to make group projects less painful
body:
Group work goes better with a little structure:

• Agree on roles in the first meeting: leader, researcher, writer, designer.
• Use one shared doc so everyone sees progress.
• Set your own deadline 2 days before the real one.
• Write down who does what. It's fairer and easier to report.

If someone isn't contributing, talk to them first, then your teacher.
why: Simple structure that saves your grade and your friendships.

title: Students these days are LAZY. Here's proof.
body:

This generation doesn't want to work. Back in my day we studied 20 hours a day and never complained.

Share this if you agree. If you're offended, you're probably one of them.
why: One random moment used to insult a whole group, so you'll comment and share in anger.

Tag a friend from the BETTER strand. Let's settle this in the comments. 🔥

We can't confirm where it came from, but share it with your classmates just in case!!
why: A 'memo' with no source or official page behind it. Check your school's official account first.

author: @viral.voicenote
title: Viral voice message: Signal No. 6 typhoon tomorrow!
body:
Forwarded many times ⏩

"My cousin works at the weather office and he says a Signal No. 6 super typhoon will hit tomorrow. The government is keeping it quiet so people won't panic. Stock up NOW and forward this to everyone you love!!"
why: There's no Signal No. 6: PAGASA's scale stops at 5. Viral voice notes aren't weather bulletins.
